sweep_summary: Single works with stress in the title: Pike & Oram 1976 (Phonetica), the primary first-hand description of Diuxi stress. Its body remains closed everywhere checked (Unpaywall closed, Karger live page PPV USD 45, SIL record 2767 links only to karger.com, archive.org has only the 1976 volume index, Karger first-page preview not archived); the abstract was re-read on the live SIL and Karger pages and matches the carried text verbatim. Nothing read contradicts the catalog: Daly 1978 p.98 (deciding source, open text) gives one grammatically predictable stress on the first syllable of the bisyllabic morpheme = stem penult, never antepenult; Hyman 2005 p.178 and Penner 2019 p.91 both report P&O 1976 (pp.321-22) as couplet-initial stress with an unpredictable second stem-final stress (on stems with reconstructed final *ʔ) that Daly reanalyzes as tone; Kuiper & Oram 1991 pp.186-187 (Oram is a P&O co-author; offprint downloaded from the Internet Archive, 234 pp, no text layer) restate the two analyses without a placement rule. The set by morphology coding stands. new_statements.quote: Each word in Diuxi Mixtec has a stressed syllable which is marked by a long vowel. In addition to this stress, some words have a second stress. This second stress occurs only on the last syllable of the word and is marked by intensity and by allotones of both high and low tone. There is a contrast of high versus low tone, and there are allotones which occur in relation to the presence versus absence of word-final stress.
new_statements.citation: Pike, Eunice V. & Joy Oram. 1976. Stress and tone in the phonology of Diuxi Mixtec. Phonetica 33(5):321-333, abstract (read on the live SIL archive record and the live Karger page; identical to the 2018 Karger snapshot already carried)
new_statements.reading: First-hand: exactly one stressed (vowel-lengthened) syllable per word, plus, in some words, a lexically restricted second stress confined to the word-final syllable, cued by intensity and tonal allotones. The abstract itself does not locate the primary stress; the placement rule (stem penult = couplet-initial, never antepenult, enclitics outside the count) is known through Daly 1978 p.98 and Penner 2019 p.91 (citing P&O pp.321-322), both consistent with the catalog's set by morphology coding.

new_statements.quote: In the Mixtec dialects/languages stems are generally disyllabic ("couplets"), with stress on their first syllable. Such stem-initial stress often conditions lengthening of the first vowel or second consonant. Certain dialects, however, have been claimed to have potentially two stresses per stem or word. According to E. Pike & Oram (1976), a second unpredictable stress occurs on the second syllable of some, but not all stems in Diuxi Mixtec—specifically on those for which a final *ʔ has been reconstructed. Just as final ˈL in Chasu is suspect, the alleged stem-final stresses in Diuxi have been reanalyzed in terms of tone (Daly 1978).

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing statement (one stressed, vowel-lengthened syllable per word = stem/couplet-initial = penult of the couplet; Pike & Oram's second stress restricted to the final syllable) and adds (a) the general Mixtec framing (couplet-initial stress with lengthening), (b) the historical conditioning of the second stress (*ʔ-final stems), and (c) an explicit judgement that the second stress is a tonal phenomenon (Daly 1978), which supports treating Diuxi as a single-stress language with a fixed stem-initial stress plus lexical tone. Note the scanned rendered the glottal-stop symbol as '*/'; the printed text has *ʔ.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Secondary source. Stress falls on the first syllable of the disyllabic stem (couplet), i.e. the stem-penult, and typically lengthens that vowel; the additional 'second stress' on the final syllable of some stems reported by Pike & Oram 1976 (historically those with reconstructed final glottal stop) is, following Daly 1978, better analysed as tone, not a second stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Discusses Pike & Oram's claimed second, unpredictable stress on the second (final) syllable of some stems; Hyman treats this claim as dubious and accepts Daly 1978's reanalysis of it as tonal.
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the stem-final 'second stress' set, which Hyman reanalyses as tone.
new_statements.identity_note: All works concern the Diuxi (Diuxi-Tilantongo) variety of Mixtec [xtd], as described by Pike & Oram 1976 and Daly 1978; Hyman's passage is explicitly about Diuxi Mixtec, prefaced by a generalisation over Mixtec varieties (couplet-initial stress). The Oram 1970 thesis (SIL entry 9966) is catalogued under Diuxi-Tilantongo Mixtec [xtd] but could not be opened.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement among the sources opened. Hyman 2006 reports the first-hand descriptions consistently: Pike & Oram 1976 place the obligatory stress on the first syllable of the disyllabic stem (the couplet-initial = stem-penultimate syllable, marked by vowel length) and claim a second, lexically restricted stress on the final syllable of some stems; Daly 1978 (already in the catalog's source folder, p.98: stress 'present always on the penultimate syllable and always absent on the antepenultimate syllable', one stress per word) reanalyses that second stress as tone, and Hyman endorses the reanalysis. The only difference is analytic (whether the final-syllable prominence is a second stress or tone), not a difference in where the primary stress falls; the catalog's 'set by morphology' coding and the existing statement are unaffected.

sources.quote: Two analyses have been proposed for the tone system of this language, one by Pike and Oram (1976), and one by Daly (1978). In the Pike and Oram system, there are two levels of tone, high and low, and also a contrastive stress. In the Daly system, there are two tone features, [High] and [Modified], which define four tones in underlying forms. ... An acute accent is used for high tone, a macron for mid tone, a circumflex for a high downglide, and a vertical stroke for stress; low tone is unmarked.
sources.note: Oram (co-author of P&O 1976) restates the two analyses (H/L tone + contrastive stress vs. [High]/[Modified] four tones) and marks stress with a vertical stroke in both notations; no statement of where the predictable stress falls.
